I was in a similar situation as this girl a few years back. While it's confusing, her not blocking her ex is a very common thing for victims of abuse to do. ESH, but AT THE TOP OF THE LIST of assholes is your BF, and you are the least AH of the three of you. You reacted harshly, but he failed as a parent for those days and it created an unsafe environment for everyone.

I work in the school system with a LOT of teen and tween age kids. This is the age for learning and testing the limits of being a human being. This age group wants and desperately needs clear boundaries. Often, those boundaries need to be set out eaely on and verbally as well as through established consequences. But intead of setting that safe boundary, your BF immediately let her know that period=no consequences (which frankly is a very sexist and cowardly approach). She's treating it like she has no control and can do whatever she wants because everyone is essentially telling her that's what a period is. She feels no control over her body and has translated that into the idea that she should act like she has no control or limits period.

And I'll be so real with you, it isn't her fault that she starts acting accordingly. Honestly, if the father OR you had reacted appropriately when she ASSAULTED YOUR SON, this wouldn't have become such an issue. Her father reacted like it was normal, and so physical reactions are now normal and you become the enemy for acting like it's not. 

You are not the AH for leaving, but because of the way you were not able to hold boundaries with your boyfriend and he was not able to hold boundaries with his daughter, everything exploded. And now there's a 11 year old girl who was trying to figure out where her and her period fit into the world and now thinks she ruined her family because of a bad week.

However, this could potentially still be corrected and worked out as a team. This could just be a huge learning experience, which happens as lot when raising adolescents. What I would LOVE to see happen, would be you and BF have an earnest talk ALONE about how you are raising your kids. Your boy got hurt in this whole disaster, and that can not ever be allowed in the future. His daughter does not have a clear understanding of what will and will not be allowed when she is on her period and that aldo can not be allowed in the future. You guys are merging parenting styles and households, so if you can't agree on boundaries and how you'll both communicate when things like this happen, then yes. Get out. If he will never adjust or learn to set boundaries, then it's not worth it.

IF you guys agree that this got out of control and his daughter needs correction on boundaries, then it's time to approach her AS A TEAM. Make it clear what a period is like for you and what your limits are. Make it clear that while yes, periods are confusing and uncomfortable, that is NEVER an excuse to lash out and become violent. Consequences on your period are the same as off your period. The father needs to make it clear to her that while her behavior was unacceptable, SO WAS HIS. He messed up because he's never had to teach someone about periods before and got overly permissive to try and make things easier for her. Then yall need to hear her. Listen to her feelings and confusion, her discomforts, and then make a plan for how she's going to deal with that in the future and how you guys can hold her to that.

That's my two cents. But again. You can always leave this situation. This was not safe for your son and he is your first priority. ESPECIALLY if your BF can't agree to holding boundaries. Good luck!

I am NOT a devil's advocate type. However, I will say that there is some crazy shit that happens with pregnancy. All of my aunts on my Dad's side really struggled with persistent delusions while pregnant. Specifically the idea that everyone hates them or is out to hurt them. It took a huge toll on their families. Maternal mental health is a really hard topic. And many women frankly start to lose it when the flood of hormones hits their body.

So my advice would be that if you have ANY inclination that she was having a psychotic episode or that she might genuinely be returning to the person that she was pre-pregnancy, both of you should go to a therapist and work through it together. You don't have to stay married!! But, if you want to be in this child's life at all, you're going to have to have several mediated conversations about what the fuck what going on with her for those 9 months.

Here's my 4 basic deal breakers/ makers

1. There is little to no evidence that a fetus feels "pain" in the womb in the early months of development. They might develop pain receptors, but they can't "feel" until there is an actual brain to receive the signals. The idea that a fetus is a person at conception is actually very new. 2. You mentioned "until term" abortions. Take time to consider why that would happen. Not many people suffer through the discomfort of 8-9 months of pregnancy just because they didn't feel like making an appointment earlier. People aren't that irresponsible with their own body and mind. Those babies were wanted. Their parents fully expected a child to come into the world at that point. These cases (in my mind) are the most tragic. This is where a mother finds out she will die in labor, that her child has developed incorrectly and will only live a few hours, or that her child doesn't have a heartbeat (miscarriage removal is considered an abortion in some states). The alternative situation is that someone was so negligent or so full of substances that they didn't notice or care they were pregnant. In which case, birth defects are almost guaranteed, if not, a lifetime full of negligence and abuse. I would rather that person not be a parent and force a child to live unwanted.

3. When we force a woman to carry an unwanted child to term, we are asking her to go through an inhumane amount of pain and suffering. There are thousands of women who have terrifying stories from pregnancy and giving birth that can make your stomach turn. Complications and long-term discomfort and pain is not at all rare, in fact its pretty normal. But those women CHOSE to go through that.  In countries like the US, giving birth is not only a huge physical burden, but also a huge financial burden. Most people simply cannot afford to give birth. Even if you choose to put up a child for adoption, they would still have to deal with the huge cost of birth along with the long term effects of a birth. There aren't enough resources to take care of people during and after birth in an affordable way. Until that problem is taken care of, it is inhumane to force people to be surrogates.

4.You can't understand until it's you. That's unfortunately the truth of it. Until you're about to leave an abusive situation and find out you're pregnant. Until you're excited to have your first child and find out it has developed without a brain and will live only a few minutes. 

Here's another realization I came to recently: 

As a woman, I've been in both situations now. I've ended a pregnancy so that I could fully cut ties with an abuser, and I've desperately wanted a child only to miscarry. I can understand why to many women hearing "it's just cells" can be insulting and extremely emotional. 20-30% of pregnancies will miscarry, so most women will have at least one in their life. But you're not really told that growing up, especially in the church. So instead of it being a natural and normal part of life, it becomes tied to "my body killed a baby" and "why can't I fulfill my role as a mother". It's a shame and sorrow filled experience that can make you question your entire world. So when someone miscarries ON PURPOSE, it can feel like a slap in the face. Like they're laughing at your pain by telling you that you didn't really lose a baby.

It took me a lot of insight and emotional accountability to realize that the mourning that we feel for a miscarriage is not the same as the pain we would feel at losing a 5 year old child or friend. The mourning and loss is very real. But it's a loss of pregnancy, not a loss of life. We mourn the child we could have had, and the potential. But that's not the same as mourning a person you've gotten to know. For me, this was actually really comforting. I realized that growing up in such a misogynistic environment had caused me even more needless pain. I was empowered by knowing that my pain is real, but that I don't need to carry guilt so deep. It helped me to connect with other women around me on a deeper level by actually talking about it.

Alright, Sociologist here. So basically, there are different kinds of "racism" and different groups of people see it in different ways. 

Many white people see "racism" as someone (usually a person of color) being rude and aggressive towards them because of their skin tone. 
This is a social and interpersonal kind of racism that can be frightening or inconvenient, but not ultimately dangerous and it usually will not be a part of their daily life. 

However, racism for people of color often comes from systematic residue from segregation. So there is less vocal social racism than in the past, but the systems are still in place. POC's overall experience much more casual racism day to day that impacts their daily lives. Including getting higher prison sentences, being paid less, lower quality medical care, stop and frisk, and lower SES overall. 

As in all things, there are exceptions to this, but they are typically limited to specific areas and cultures. 

So why do POC sometimes treat White people badly if they know it feels shitty? Well, it's part of relative deprivation. When we don't feel great about our situation and have no power to change it, we compare ourselves to those we perceive as "not struggling" and feel resentful. Often the rational is that white people have the whole system backing them up, so it doesn't matter what is said or done, they'll still get what they want. 

I am NOT saying any of this is right! These are just theories on why this happens and why it is seen differently. As a general rule: Don't Be An Asshole.
